strengths: Simple, cleanly motivated, and practically useful idea: replacing 3DGS's iterative densification with a one-shot dense initialization obtained by triangulating dense 2D correspondences (RoMa). The method is drop-in compatible with existing pipelines, as demonstrated by combining it with Taming-3DGS.

Thorough and largely fair empirical evaluation: three standard datasets (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), per-scene results in the supplement, retrained baselines (3DGS*, Scaffold-GS under matched settings), and—importantly—the one-time cost of dense correspondence computation is included in the reported training times.

Consistent evidence for the central claims: better SSIM/LPIPS, ~40–60% fewer Gaussians, and faster convergence (Ours 5K is competitive with efficiency-focused methods), supported by qualitative results showing sharper high-frequency detail (flowers, treehill) and more stable extreme-viewpoint rendering (Fig. 4).

Solid ablation suite that isolates the contribution: matching backbone comparison (RoMa/LoFTR/DKM/RAFT), depth-based alternative (DepthFM), noise robustness for coordinates vs. colors, hyperparameter sensitivity (number of reference views/keypoints), densification on/off (Table 2), and quantitative analysis of Gaussian displacement/trajectory length during optimization (Fig. 5).

Clear presentation and reasonably honest discussion of limitations (reflective surfaces, under-covered regions, dependence on dense coverage), with useful supplementary diagnostics (confidence aggregation, per-scene tables, notation table).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: initializing 3DGS from dense correspondences/triangulation rather than SfM points has been explored before (e.g., RAIN-GS, RadSplat, InstantSplat-style dense/sparse-view initializations). The paper's positioning against these is shallow—InstantSplat is cited but never compared—so the incremental contribution is mostly the 'no densification at all' regime plus the demonstration, rather than a new formulation.

The headline performance claim needs more nuance: PSNR is essentially on par or slightly lower than 3DGS* on several scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF360 27.80 vs 27.81; Tanks&Temples 28.06 vs 28.15), so the 'outperforms quality-focused SOTA' claim rests mainly on SSIM/LPIPS. Likewise the 30K speedup is modest (29 min vs 42 min on Mip-NeRF360), while much faster baselines (MiniSplatting, ~12 min) remain far ahead, albeit at lower quality.

Potential inconsistency between the Fig. 1 claim ('reaches the original 3DGS LPIPS score in just 25% of the training time') and Table 1, where the 5K model has LPIPS 0.302 vs. 3DGS's 0.214 and PSNR 26.70 vs. 27.81. The paper should clarify whether comparisons are at equal wall-clock time or equal step count; as written, a reader could be misled about the 5K model's parity.

Robustness to inputs is under-examined. The method inherits the accuracy of COLMAP poses and the dense matcher, but there is no evaluation under pose/calibration noise, imperfect SfM, or sparse-view settings (only mentioned briefly in the supplement). Failure modes (specular/reflective surfaces, under-covered regions, Fig. A6) are acknowledged but not quantified.

Several design choices are heuristic and tuned ad hoc—scale from distance to nearest camera, identity rotation, averaging matched-pixel colors, 180 reference views/15K keypoints—without principled justification or a fully unsupervised/self-tuning alternative; the sensitivity curves help but do not resolve this.

The densification-free design can be a liability where coverage is poor (the paper itself shows densification helps on under-initialized scenes such as treehill), which somewhat undercuts the strong 'eliminate densification entirely' framing.

strengths: The proposed dense initialization is simple and effective: triangulating dense 2D correspondences and disabling densification yields strong empirical gains, e.g., on Mip-NeRF360 Ours+3DGS 30K improves LPIPS from 0.214 (3DGS) to 0.175, reduces training time from 42m to 29m, and uses 1.9M vs 3.5M Gaussians.
The method is orthogonal to existing 3DGS accelerations and can be combined with them; Ours+Taming 3DGS further improves quality and speed, demonstrating practical versatility.

Evaluation is broad across three standard datasets with multiple baselines (3DGS, 3DGS-LM, Taming 3DGS, gsplat, Mip-Splatting, Scaffold-GS, 3DGS-MCMC, MiniSplatting, etc.) and includes per-scene results in the supplementary.

Ablations are informative: matching algorithm comparison, noise robustness, hyperparameter sensitivity, densification effect, Gaussian motion/path length analysis, and extreme viewpoint rendering support the core claims.
The paper is generally clear, with implementation details, optimization protocol, hardware, and notation table provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the idea of replacing sparse SfM initialization with dense matching/triangulation and turning off densification is a straightforward pipeline rather than a fundamentally new algorithm; it relies heavily on a pretrained dense matcher (RoMa), which may be viewed as an empirical recipe.

The method's initialization quality and cost depend on the dense matching network; the paper does not deeply analyze failure modes (e.g., textureless regions, repeated structures) or scalability to very large scenes, and memory usage (15GB peak) may limit applicability.

Some claims are overstated: on Mip-NeRF360, PSNR/SSIM are slightly below 3DGS-MCMC (27.80/0.840 vs 28.15/0.842), so 'higher rendering quality' is metric- and dataset-dependent; the abstract's broad claim should be qualified.

Fairness of timing comparisons is not fully transparent: for most baselines SfM/COLMAP time is excluded, while EDGS includes dense matching time; several baseline numbers are taken from prior papers with different training steps/hardware, and retraining is limited.

Technical clarity issues remain: it is unclear how 'densification disabled' interacts with pruning, since Fig. A5 shows the Gaussian count decreasing; scale/rotation initialization is heuristic (identity rotation, nearest-camera distance) and lacks ablation beyond noise analysis.

Evaluation breadth is still limited to 13 scenes from three datasets, with no large-scale or sparse-view stress test; no comparison to feed-forward dense-view Gaussian initialization alternatives, and the impact of the matching confidence threshold/outlier rejection is not fully explored.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, practical initialization strategy for 3DGS: dense 2D correspondences from a pretrained matcher are triangulated to initialize Gaussians, avoiding the usual iterative densification and shortening the optimization path.

It evaluates on three standard datasets (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) against many baselines and includes qualitative comparisons, ablations on matching algorithms, initialization type, noise robustness, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
The method can be combined with existing accelerators such as Taming 3DGS, and the paper provides some evidence for faster convergence and fewer Gaussians in several settings.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The paper claims to 'consistently outperform all other techniques,' but on Mip-NeRF360 3DGS-MCMC achieves better PSNR and SSIM than the proposed method (28.15/0.842 vs. 27.80/0.840). The claim of 'eliminating densification entirely' is weakened by Table 2, where adding densification still improves the authors' own initialization (e.g., PSNR 27.80 to 27.84), and by the supplementary note that densification can help in under-covered scenes.

There are technical inconsistencies and reproducibility gaps. In Table 1, 'Ours + 3DGS 5K steps' reports 2.9M Gaussians while 'Ours + 3DGS 30K steps' reports 1.9M, even though densification is disabled; this is not explained and undermines the efficiency claims. The exact initial scale formula, opacity initialization, confidence threshold for keypoint sampling, and breakdown of matching/initialization time are not specified. The triangulation derivation in Eqs. (4)-(7) is dimensionally unclear and hard to reproduce.

Novelty is limited. Dense matching followed by triangulation is standard in SfM/MVS pipelines; applying it as a 3DGS initialization is an incremental combination of existing components. The paper does not compare against other dense-initialization or feed-forward Gaussian methods such as InstantSplat or RAD-Splat, relying mainly on RoMa and DepthFM comparisons.

The evaluation has important limitations. It assumes known camera poses and dense view overlap, and robustness is tested only with synthetic Gaussian noise rather than realistic matching outliers. The method's scalability to large scenes is not demonstrated; the hyperparameter study uses up to 180 reference cameras, which may be impractical. Timing comparisons are also not fully apples-to-apples because baseline training times exclude their initialization cost while the proposed method includes dense correspondence computation.

Ablation and analysis claims are under-supported. Figure 5 asserts 50x/30x reductions in parameter movement but provides no numerical summary; Figure 6's noise robustness conclusions are qualitative; and integration with Taming 3DGS does not consistently reduce Gaussian count or improve time over Taming alone (e.g., 16m vs. 14m on Mip-NeRF360).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated idea: replacing slow incremental densification in 3DGS with a one-step dense initialization derived from triangulated 2D correspondences is a sensible and practically useful direction.

The method is described with sufficient technical detail (triangulation formulation, sampling distribution combining confidence and re-projection terms, spherical harmonics initialization) and the supplementary provides implementation specifics (timings, GPU memory, thresholds), aiding reproducibility.

Empirical evaluation is broad: three standard datasets, comparisons to 3DGS, AbsGS, Rain-GS, Mip-Splatting, 3DGS-MCMC, Scaffold-GS, Taming 3DGS, EAGLES, and 3DGS-LM, plus per-scene results in the supplement.

Ablations are thorough and informative: matching-network comparison, sampling-distribution component ablation, SH initialization, different initialization strategies (random/COLMAP/DepthFM), noise robustness, hyperparameter sensitivity, and an analysis of Gaussian parameter motion during optimization.

Demonstrates plug-and-play compatibility with adaptive density control methods (Table 3) and includes a sparse-view evaluation (Table A1), showing the initialization transfers beyond a single pipeline.
weaknesses: The 'efficiency' framing is not consistently supported by the reported wall-clock numbers: on Tanks&Temples EDGS reports 23m vs. 3DGS at 18m, i.e., slower training despite better quality, and the abstract's '15% of training time' claim relies on selective comparison. The full pipeline also depends on COLMAP/SfM camera poses whose cost is not accounted for in the efficiency claims.

Initialization cost is substantial (~120s end-to-end on A100, dominated by ~76s of dense matching with a pretrained RoMa network). Because matching scales with the number of reference/neighbor pairs, the initialization overhead may grow unfavorably with scene size, and the paper does not analyze this scaling.

The 'state-of-the-art quality' claim is overstated: EDGS does not lead on PSNR on Mip-NeRF360 (28.02 vs. 3DGS-MCMC 28.15), so the advantage is largely on perceptual metrics (LPIPS/SSIM). This distinction should be stated more carefully.

Baseline fairness is questionable in places: the retrained 3DGS* is reported at unusually low PSNR on Tanks&Temples (21.34) relative to commonly reported figures, and some comparison rows are taken from prior papers or evaluated under differing resolutions/hardware, which complicates direct claims of superiority.

The 'eliminating densification' narrative is somewhat weakened by the ADC-integration experiments (Table 3), where densification is still enabled and final Gaussian counts are kept comparable by using fewer initial points; this should be framed as a design choice rather than a strict elimination in all settings.

Robustness of the method depends on the quality of pretrained dense matching and on overlapping views; the paper does not adequately characterize failure modes in textureless regions, limited-overlap captures, or scenes where matching is unreliable.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated idea with a strong practical payoff: the paper shows that dense correspondence-based initialization can replace incremental densification entirely, and the resulting EDGS+3DGS achieves best or second-best PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS across all three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending) with comparable Gaussian counts and no densification. This is a meaningful result given densification is a known bottleneck of 3DGS.

The method is convincingly shown to be a plug-and-play initialization: Table 3 demonstrates consistent improvements when EDGS initialization is combined with ADC methods (AbsGS, 3DGS-MCMC, Taming 3DGS) without extra hyperparameter tuning, and Table 5 shows it is robust to the choice of matching algorithm (LoFTR, DKM, RoMa), which strengthens generality.

Analysis is thorough and directly supports the central claim: Gaussian motion/convergence analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 4) quantifies that EDGS initializes closer to the final solution (50x smaller coordinate displacement, 30x shorter trajectory), the sampling-distribution ablation (Table 6) isolates the contribution of the confidence and reprojection terms, and the noise-robustness study (Fig. 7) and initialization-type comparison (Table 7) provide useful context against SfM and depth-based baselines.

Reproducibility is strong: implementation details, matching/confidence/reprojection thresholds, SH initialization via pseudoinverse, and time/memory breakdowns are given in the supplement, and competing methods are re-evaluated on the same hardware with a retrained 3DGS* baseline that is honestly reported as outperforming its original numbers.
Well-structured paper with clear figures and a notation table (Table A9) that aids understanding.
weaknesses: The initialization cost is substantial and the efficiency claim is partly offset by it. The default full-scene initialization takes ~120s on an A100, dominated by ~76s of dense matching, plus ~15GB peak GPU memory during initialization. In Table 2, EDGS + 3DGS 10K requires 23m total versus 16m for 3DGS-LM and 14m for Taming 3DGS, so the total wall-clock advantage over the fastest competing methods is not always realized despite faster convergence.

There is an unexplained numerical inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 2: EDGS + 3DGS at 30K reports PSNR 28.02 (Table 1) while the 10K variant reports 28.34 (Table 2), i.e., the longer run has lower PSNR but higher SSIM. This discrepancy is not discussed and raises questions about stability/configuration differences that should be clarified.

The contribution is arguably more of a well-executed pipeline/engineering improvement (swap SfM initialization for dense-matching-based dense initialization) than a fundamentally new algorithm; the reliance on a heavy pretrained matcher (RoMa) means the quality ceiling is partly inherited from that model, and the method inherits the cost of that model.

The dependence on the matching network is acknowledged but not fully characterized in failure cases: the paper notes RAFT degrades due to its optical-flow design, but does not analyze scenes where matching confidence is low (e.g., textureless or highly reflective regions), which could limit real-world robustness.

The densification-elimination framing is slightly nuanced: Table 3 shows EDGS is also used together with densification-based methods, and the isolated contribution of initialization versus the retained ADC machinery is only partially disentangled; a cleaner comparison of EDGS-only vs. ADC-only under matched Gaussian budgets would strengthen the central claim.

strengths: The core idea — replacing 3DGS's incremental densification with a dense, correspondence-triangulated initialization — is simple, well-motivated, and empirically effective: EDGS+3DGS reaches SSIM 0.839 / LPIPS 0.141 on Mip-NeRF360 vs 0.815 / 0.215 for retrained 3DGS, and is best or near-best on all three metrics across three datasets (Table 1).

The method is genuinely plug-and-play: Table 3 shows that using EDGS as an initialization consistently improves AbsGS, 3DGS-MCMC and Taming 3DGS without increasing final Gaussian count or training time, which is a practically useful property.

The ablation suite is broad: matching backbone comparison (RoMa/LoFTR/DKM/RAFT, Table 5), sampling-distribution components (Table 6), SH initialization, noise robustness (Fig. 7), alternative initialization strategies including dense COLMAP and DepthFM (Table 7, Table A2), and a sparse-view evaluation (Table A1).

Early-stopping results (Table 2) support the convergence claim: EDGS+3DGS 5K (8 min) matches or beats EAGLES, Taming 3DGS, gsplat and MiniSplatting on two of three metrics at lower or comparable time.

Implementation details (thresholds τ_corr=0.05, τ_proj=0.01, number of reference views, per-stage timings, GPU memory, optimization schedule) are reported in the supplement, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is questionable and the positioning is incomplete. Dense/MVS-based point-cloud initialization for 3DGS already exists in prior/concurrent work (e.g., InstantSplat, cited here only as 'sparse-view pose-free' although it initializes from a dense stereo point cloud; MVS-GS; dense COLMAP/MVS point clouds). The Related Work section only covers RAIN-GS, 3DGS-MCMC and RadSplat and never engages with the dense-initialization line of research, so the claim of a 'novel dense initialization' is not substantiated.

The efficiency claim is overstated and contradicted by the paper's own numbers. Table 1 shows EDGS+3DGS takes 27 min on Mip-NeRF360 vs 26 min for retrained 3DGS (23 vs 19 min on Tanks&Temples, 30 vs 28 min on Deep Blending), i.e., total wall-clock time is not improved. The '8x faster' / '15% of training time' claims in Fig. 1 and the abstract refer only to reaching a fixed quality target, and initialization alone costs ~120 s of GPU time (≈76 s of RoMa forward passes plus ~26 s triangulation/SH), a non-trivial cost that grows with the number of reference views.

A natural and strong baseline is missing: initializing from a COLMAP dense MVS (patch-match stereo) point cloud. The paper only scales up COLMAP *sparse* points (Table A2) and compares against DepthFM monocular depth; without a dense-MVS baseline one cannot tell whether the gains come from the specific confidence/reprojection sampling or simply from having any dense geometric initialization.

The contribution is narrower than the title suggests: 'eliminating densification' is really 'better initialization', and the method still relies on the standard 3DGS optimization; Tables 3–4 show densification still adds value when enabled, so the framing oversells the result.

Scalability of the initialization is not addressed: dense matching cost is linear in the number of reference views (180×2 RoMa passes ≈76 s on an A100) and 20K correspondences per view × 180 views yields millions of candidate points. Behavior on larger scenes or image collections is not evaluated.

Quantitative reporting is incomplete: no variance or error bars across runs, and per-scene tables (Tables A4–A8) show mixed outcomes (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC+EDGS Init beats EDGS+3DGS on SSIM for bicycle/flowers/garden/stump), which is not discussed.

Comparison provenance is muddled: footnotes indicate some numbers are taken directly from papers and some from an A6000 vs A100, making the headline 'fastest / most efficient' claims hard to reconcile with a fair same-hardware comparison.
